summary: Cycloserine is a second-line oral antituberculosis agent used to treat active pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB (including MDR-TB) when primary drugs (streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol) are inadequate, and only as part of a multidrug regimen. Its defining hazard is dose-related CNS/neuropsychiatric toxicity - convulsions, psychosis (possibly with suicidal tendencies), depression, confusion, somnolence, tremor, and paresis - which closely tracks excessive blood levels above 30 mcg/mL from high dosage or inadequate renal clearance. The toxic-to-effective dose ratio is small, so serum levels must be monitored and kept below 30 mcg/mL. It is contraindicated in epilepsy, depression/severe anxiety/psychosis, severe renal insufficiency, and excessive alcohol use. Pyridoxine is often co-administered and can help treat/prevent neurotoxicity. Discontinue or reduce dose if CNS toxicity or allergic dermatitis develops.
indications: Active pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis (including renal TB) caused by susceptible organisms when treatment with primary medications (streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol) has proved inadequate - always combined with other effective chemotherapy
Acute urinary tract infections caused by susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, only when conventional therapy has failed and susceptibility is demonstrated

moa: Cycloserine is a structural analog of D-alanine. Its antibacterial activity results from inhibition of bacterial cell-wall synthesis in susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis. By competitively inhibiting the enzymes alanine racemase (which converts L-alanine to D-alanine) and D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase, it blocks incorporation of D-alanine into the peptidoglycan pentapeptide, impairing cross-linking and weakening the cell wall. Its CNS toxicity reflects activity at neuronal receptors (it is a partial agonist at the NMDA-receptor glycine site), accounting for the prominent neuropsychiatric adverse effects.

History of vitamin B12 / folic-acid deficiency or anemia
monitor: Serum cycloserine blood levels (keep below 30 mcg/mL)

preg: Pregnancy Category C. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; rat studies up to 100 mg/kg/day (approximately the maximum recommended human dose on a body-surface-area basis) showed no teratogenic effect. Cycloserine crosses the placenta - fetal blood concentrations approach maternal serum levels. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Cycloserine is excreted into breast milk, with milk concentrations approaching those found in serum. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, taking into account the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Cycloserine is substantially excreted by the kidney (about 65% recovered unchanged in urine within 72 hours). It is contraindicated in severe renal insufficiency. In reduced renal function, inadequate clearance causes accumulation and toxic blood levels (above 30 mcg/mL); determine blood levels at least weekly and reduce the dose to keep levels below 30 mcg/mL. Caution and renal monitoring are advised in the elderly.
hepatic: Elevated serum transaminases have been reported, especially in patients with preexisting liver disease. Monitor liver function studies during therapy.

major: Alcohol - incompatible with cycloserine; increases the possibility and risk of epileptic (seizure) episodes, especially with large doses
moderate: Isoniazid - may increase incidence of CNS effects such as dizziness or drowsiness; monitor closely and adjust dose as needed
Other CNS-active drugs / sedatives - additive CNS effects (also used therapeutically to control toxicity symptoms)
minor: Other antituberculosis drugs - association with vitamin B12 and/or folic-acid deficiency and anemia in a few instances
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to food; absorption is readily achieved from the GI tract.
interactions.alcohol: Contraindicated with excessive use; alcohol is incompatible with cycloserine and increases the risk of seizures.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause elevated serum transaminases; monitor LFTs. Hematologic changes (megaloblastic/sideroblastic anemia) may occur.

counsel: Take exactly as prescribed and always alongside your other TB medicines - never stop on your own
Tell your clinician immediately about seizures, severe mood changes, depression, thoughts of self-harm, confusion, or unusual behavior
Avoid alcohol completely - it raises the risk of seizures
Report rash, tremor, numbness/tingling, headache, or drowsiness
Attend regular blood tests, including drug levels, kidney, blood count, and liver tests
Take pyridoxine (vitamin B6) if prescribed - it can help reduce nervous-system side effects
Use caution driving or operating machinery if drowsy or dizzy

pearls: Defining hazard is dose-related CNS/neuropsychiatric toxicity - seizures, psychosis with suicidal tendencies, depression, confusion - tracking blood levels above 30 mcg/mL
Narrow therapeutic index: keep serum levels below 30 mcg/mL with weekly monitoring (esp. renal impairment or >500 mg/day)
Contraindicated in epilepsy, depression/anxiety/psychosis, severe renal insufficiency, and excessive alcohol use
Pyridoxine 200-300 mg/day can help prevent and treat neurotoxicity (and is used in overdose)
Renally cleared - reduce dose or avoid in renal impairment; accumulation drives toxicity
Always part of a multidrug TB regimen, never monotherapy; confirm susceptibility first
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once - higher blood levels increase the risk of seizures and other nervous-system effects.
overdose: Acute toxicity can occur if more than 1 g is ingested by an adult; chronic toxicity is dose-related and can occur above 500 mg daily. The CNS is the most commonly affected system: headache, vertigo, confusion, drowsiness, hyperirritability, paresthesias, dysarthria, psychosis, paresis, convulsions, and coma. Treatment: administer pyridoxine 200-300 mg daily, which can both treat and prevent many neurotoxic effects; provide supportive and anticonvulsant care. Hemodialysis removes cycloserine and should be reserved for life-threatening toxicity unresponsive to less invasive therapy.
